entities.summary:
The Statue of Liberty, officially named 'Liberty Enlightening the World,' was dedicated on October 28, 1886, and stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. Designed by French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi and engineered by Gustave Eiffel, this colossal statue symbolizes freedom and democracy, embodying the values of the United States and serving as a welcoming beacon to millions of immigrants arriving by sea. Its significance transcends national borders, representing a universal ideal of liberty and hope during a pivotal time in world history, particularly as the United States emerged as a global power.

The statue was a gift from France to the United States, a gesture meant to commemorate the centennial of American independence and celebrate the enduring friendship between the two nations. Funded through extensive public donations and organized by journalist Joseph Pulitzer, the statue was constructed in France and then disassembled, shipped to America, and reassembled on its pedestal designed by Richard Morris Hunt. The dedication ceremony was attended by thousands, signifying a moment of unity and celebration of democratic principles.

The legacy of the Statue of Liberty has been profound; it has inspired countless movements advocating for civil rights and social justice. The statue has become an enduring symbol of hope for immigrants and has been referenced in various cultural and political contexts as a representation of the American Dream. The phrase 'Give me your tired, your poor,' from Emma Lazarus's poem inscribed at its base, encapsulates the welcoming spirit of the United States and reflects the ongoing dialogue about immigration and national identity.
